Since x≠0, u≠1, so the line through (1,1) and (u,v) has finite rational slope t=(v−1)/(u−1). Its second intersection with the circle gives the displayed parametrization; writing t=m/n in lowest terms yields the claimed formula, with m≠0 and m≠±n."},{"claim":"The reduced denominator is r², where r=q/gcd(q,2), and r is odd, at least 5, with all prime divisors 1 modulo 4.","reasoning":"For odd p dividing q, neither m nor n is divisible by p, and p cannot also divide n²−m²: the two congruences would imply 2m²≡0 modulo p. If q is even, m,n are odd, q≡2 modulo 8, and 8 divides n²−m², so cancellation against q² at 2 is exactly 4. These facts give the denominator formula. Any odd p dividing r makes −1 a quadratic residue modulo p. The excluded cases m=±n and the elementary lower bounds for sums of two nonzero squares give r≥5."},{"claim":"The reduced numerator is divisible by 24.","reasoning":"If q is odd, mn is even, giving a factor 8 in N; if q is even, n²−m² is divisible by 8 and cancellation by 4 still leaves a factor 8. Modulo 3, either 3 divides mn or the nonzero squares m²,n² agree, so 3 divides N. In the even-q case 3 cannot divide q for primitive m,n; in the odd-q case no odd prime factor of q cancels against N. Thus the reduced numerator retains divisibility by both 8 and 3."},{"claim":"These restrictions do not resolve the four-neighbor mutual-edge conditions or the main sextuple problem.","reasoning":"The final reformulation makes each mutual edge equivalent to u_i u_j+r_i²r_j² being a square, but supplies neither a contradiction nor a construction satisfying all six equations.
